summary:
SARAURA is an open-source web app that turns NASA-ISRO NISAR radar into plain answers to the questions people ask about a place: “Is it safe to build here?”, “Which burned slopes could send mud onto villages this winter?”, “Where did the flood reach, camp by camp?”. Users pick who they are (civil protection, a council, a home buyer, a camp operator) and tap any village, road or spot to see the answer, the radar measurement behind it, and what they can do.

For the “Dancing with the SARs” challenge, it tracks four kinds of surface change with NISAR L-band data: burn scars near Jijel, Algeria; subsidence in Mexico City; the Okavango Delta flood pulse in Botswana; and earthquake damage around Caracas, Venezuela. A research explorer adds every NISAR pass on a 3D globe, on-demand analysis of any area, time series, and AI models each scored against a simple baseline.

NISAR sees through cloud, smoke and darkness every 12 days, but its data comes as large HDF5 files that only specialists can read. SARAURA puts it in the hands of the people who must decide, and renews the answers with every pass.
details:
What it does. SARAURA has two halves, decisions first and research second.

  • Places and decisions. Each place opens with “Who are you?” and then the questions for that role, 20 in all across four places. Tap any village, road or spot: you get the answer there, the measurement behind it, and ranked options with their cost and source. Every place exports a PDF report.
  • Research explorer. A 3D globe shows every NISAR pass. Draw an area and an on-demand analysis processes only that area, with physics layers, time series, before/after swipes, statistics and a “why it changed” note. Model cards compare each AI model with a simple baseline.

The four places and what the radar answers there.

  • Jijel, Algeria (wildfire, Aug 2026): which villages lie below burned steep slopes that could send mud this winter, which roads to watch in heavy rain, where to replant first, which farms lost their cover, which rivers and dams receive the mud.
  • Mexico City (subsidence): is it safe to build here, what to build, better plots nearby, which Metro, rail and canal lines cross uneven sinking.
  • Okavango Delta, Botswana (flood pulse): where the flood reached, camp by camp; safe ground; water hidden under reeds; which tracks flood and when.
  • Caracas, Venezuela (M7.5 earthquake): which neighbourhoods to inspect first, where not to rebuild, ground still moving, lifelines crossed.

How it works.

  1. A Python pipeline searches NASA’s CMR catalogue and reads only the needed chunks of NISAR L2 GCOV (backscatter, polarizations) and GUNW (interferometric displacement, coherence) files from the ASF DAAC.
  2. It computes the evidence for a place once: burn and water maps, displacement rates, slope, flow paths (priority-flood routing on Copernicus GLO-30), plus OpenStreetMap villages, roads, fields and rivers.
  3. Each question is a small YAML file with stated thresholds, classes, sources and limits; a recipe reads the evidence and follows Risk = Hazard × Exposure × Vulnerability. When the evidence is weak, the answer is “not measurable”, never a guess.
  4. AI models plug in only through files (a model card plus prediction maps), are checked by a script, and are always shown next to a simple baseline.
  5. A FastAPI back end serves tiles, answers and reports; a Next.js and MapLibre front end draws the maps, 3D terrain and the scroll story.

The physics we rely on. Burned forest loses volume scattering, so cross-polarized HV backscatter drops after a fire. Open water is a mirror and returns little energy, while water under reeds returns a strong double bounce in HH. Interferometric phase (GUNW) measures centimetre-scale ground motion for subsidence and the earthquake, and loss of coherence marks damaged buildings.

How good the AI models are, honestly. Scores are on held-out spatial blocks; most labels are Sentinel-2 proxies, stated on each model card.

  • Wildfire (Jijel): U-Net 0.92 vs HV-drop rule 0.33, burned IoU
  • Farming (US Midwest): LightGBM 0.86 vs HV-variation rule 0.53, macro F1
  • Earthquake (Caracas): LightGBM + U-Net ensemble 0.73 vs coherence loss 0.61, average precision against Copernicus EMS damage grades
  • Wetland (Okavango): LightGBM + HMM 0.21 vs Otsu on HH 0.01, open-water IoU against Sentinel-2
  • Volcano (Kamchatka): LightGBM 0.07 vs largest HH change 0.003, average precision
  • Subsidence (Mexico City): LightGBM 0.68 cm vs straight-line trend 0.63 cm, RMSE three passes ahead (lower is better: the baseline wins)

The wetland maps still show more open water than Sentinel-2, so their answers say they read an AI model’s maps and should be checked on the ground.

Benefits. Plain-language answers for non-specialists, renewed every 12 days through cloud and smoke; every answer traceable to a layer and a cited rule; open source, so any agency or university can add a place or a question.

Intended impact. Before the winter rains, civil protection and councils in Jijel can see the 14 villages that lie within 250 m of a main mud path and the 115 road sections to watch in heavy rain. In Mexico City, a family can check a plot before buying; in the Okavango, camps can plan access for the flood months. Next, we want to test the Jijel answers with local civil protection and councils, add places and questions as new NISAR passes arrive, and add ISRO S-band where it covers our sites. In the long run, any agency can add its own place by writing question files, with no new code.

How it is creative.

  • It starts from the person, not the pixel. “Who are you?” comes first; the map shows only the questions for that role.
  • Answers, not maps. Each answer gives the reason, ranked options with their cost and source, and what to check on the ground.
  • Models are chained into new insight. Burn map × slope × flow routing shows which villages, roads and dams the mud reaches; a water map on every pass shows when each track floods.
  • Questions are files, not code. A question is a short YAML file with its thresholds, sources and limits, so experts can add one without programming.
  • Honesty is built in. Every AI model sits next to a simple baseline, and weak evidence gives “not measurable” instead of a guess.

Factors we considered.

  • Users with no radar training: plain words, colour-blind-safe colour maps, a caution colour kept for risk only, and a layout that works on phones.
  • Scientific honesty: proxy labels declared on every model card, scores on held-out spatial blocks, and limits written into each answer (20–80 m pixels judge a neighbourhood, not a single house).
  • Data limits: NISAR’s provisional known issues (ionosphere residuals at high latitude, calibration of the 80 m product) and the tropospheric correction not yet applied to GUNW.
  • Local knowledge: place names in Arabic and French from OpenStreetMap for Jijel [add a line on why the team chose Jijel, if it is close to home].
  • Cost and openness: free data, open source, runs on a laptop, and processes only the area asked for (up to 900 km² for GCOV, 500 km² for GUNW).
  • Ethics: no personal data and no images of people.

Tools. Python (FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, h5py, Shapely), LightGBM and PyTorch for the models, Next.js 16, React 19, MapLibre GL and three.js for the front end, Google Gemini for the in-app assistant (prototype). Hardware: a laptop with a GTX 1660 Ti GPU for training.
